issues.legal_issue: A supervisory court may interfere with concurrent factual findings when the finding under review has no evidentiary support and rests on a manifest error.
material_facts: The tenancy authorities concurrently found that the occupant was the landowner’s tenant, but he had himself claimed to occupy as a subtenant of the original tenant.
The occupant did not testify, produced no rent receipts, and relied on a son who lacked knowledge of the relevant facts.
The effective revenue-record entries showed that the occupant was not in possession as the landowner’s tenant.
The High Court set aside the authorities’ finding, and the Supreme Court held that the finding lacked evidentiary support.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted within its supervisory jurisdiction in setting aside the concurrent finding, and its judgment was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 227 of the Constitution, a High Court cannot act as an appellate court and is generally bound by a tribunal’s findings of fact; however, the concurrent finding here was unsupported by evidence, so interference was justified. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_concurrent_factual: A supervisory court is reviewing a factual finding made concurrently by lower authorities.
predicates.finding_lacks_evidentiary_support: The finding is unsupported by evidence, including where the claimant supplies no competent supporting evidence and the relevant records contradict the finding.

issues.definition: When a supervisory court reviews a concurrent factual finding that lacks evidentiary support, it may set that finding aside.

issues.legal_issue: A person cultivating land as a subtenant under a tenancy regime that prohibits subletting cannot qualify as a deemed tenant where deemed tenancy requires lawful cultivation.
material_facts: The occupant claimed that he possessed the land as a subtenant of the original tenant.
The applicable tenancy law prohibited subletting, and the tenancy was liable to termination on the ground of subletting.
The statutory route to deemed tenancy required the claimant to cultivate the land lawfully.
issues.conclusion: The occupant’s claimed status as a subtenant did not make him a deemed tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, required lawful cultivation for deemed tenancy. Section 27 invalidated subletting, and Section 14(1)(a)(iii) made a tenancy liable to termination for subletting. Read together, those provisions meant that cultivation by a subtenant was not lawful for this purpose. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: tenancy_status_determination and claimant_cultivated_as_subtenant and applicable_law_prohibits_subletting and deemed_tenancy_requires_lawful_cultivation

predicates.tenancy_status_determination: A proceeding determines whether a person occupying land qualifies as a tenant under the applicable tenancy regime.
predicates.claimant_cultivated_as_subtenant: The claimant cultivated the land under a tenant rather than directly under the landowner.
predicates.applicable_law_prohibits_subletting: The applicable tenancy regime does not permit a tenant to sublet the land.
predicates.deemed_tenancy_requires_lawful_cultivati: The applicable route to deemed tenancy requires the claimant’s cultivation to be lawful.

issues.definition: A claimant who cultivated as a subtenant is not a deemed tenant when the applicable law prohibits subletting and deemed tenancy requires lawful cultivation.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner’s statutory notice and a preliminary proceeding initiated by a tribunal do not, without a determination of tenant status, establish that an occupant is a tenant.
material_facts: The landowner served the occupant with a statutory notice.
The tribunal initiated a proceeding on its own motion concerning the statutory purchase price.
The tribunal’s order postponed the relevant date because the landowners were widows; it did not determine that the occupant was a tenant.
The proceeding was not initiated at the landowners’ instance, and there was no adverse order against them.
issues.conclusion: Neither the notice nor the preliminary tribunal proceeding established the occupant’s tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory notice may be served as a precaution and does not by itself prove a tenancy. A tribunal’s suo motu preliminary proceeding does not imply that the landowner conceded tenant status, particularly where the tribunal has not decided that status. The relevant provisions discussed are Sections 31 and 32-G of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: tenancy_status_determination and landlord_served_statutory_notice and tribunal_started_preliminary_process and tribunal_did_not_determine_tenant_status

predicates.tenancy_status_determination: A proceeding determines whether an occupant is a tenant of the landowner.
predicates.landlord_served_statutory_notice: The landowner served the occupant with a statutory notice concerning the land.
predicates.tribunal_started_preliminary_process: A tribunal began a preliminary process concerning the land, including one initiated on its own motion.
predicates.tribunal_did_not_determine_tenant_status: The tribunal’s order did not decide that the occupant was the landowner’s tenant.

issues.definition: In a tenancy-status determination, a statutory notice and a preliminary tribunal process do not establish tenancy when the tribunal did not decide tenant status.
